newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish researchers call halt to cow-cloning tests.
newsitem.headline: Danish researchers call halt to cow-cloning tests.

text.p: Danish scientists, working on cloning livestock said on Wednesday they were halting experiments on cows pending a full debate on the thorny issue in Denmark.
"We have stopped our attempt to transfer embryos using the technique where the cells from an adult animal are included," Henrik Callesen, director of the Foulum Embryo-Technology Centre told Reuters.
"We are waiting for a political, legal and ethical decision in Denmark, which we expect within some months. In the meantime we will continue laboratory work," he said.

"Another thing is that we need time to do much more basic research on this technique before any (embryo) transfer can be considered. A lot of key research can continue without actually producing a calf," he said.
In Denmark, as in other countries, the prospect of possible human cloning more than of animals is the chief moral concern.

The idea of making carbon copies of human beings crossed from the realm of science fiction to possible reality last week when a Scottish scientist introduced the world to Dolly, a lamb cloned from an adult sheep.
"The similarity between our work and the Scottish experiment is that we used cells from an adult animal as part of the cloning process, but the actual process might well be different," Callesen said.
He said his team's experiments centred on attempts to plant eggs, taken from newly dead cows, in an incubator.

"The egg placed in an incubator at our first attempt last week probably only divided a couple of times. Even if it had developed completely we would not have continued to attempt to produce a calf," he said.

"It was just an initial laboratory experiment, there was no question of transferring an embryo. Even if it is in the incubator for a short time - up to two weeks - it will provide important information about the success of the process used," Callesen added.

Callesen said successful cloning of farm animals could be of potential benefit to agriculture, providing another tool in modern cattle breeding along with accepted methods such as articial insemination.

Cloning has caused a controversy in many countries, notably the United States where President Bill Clinton on Tuesday banned federally-funded human cloning and asked private scientists voluntarily to enact a similar moratorium while government advisers review the ethically troublesome issue.
